That sounds like a horrible monster.

Not like horrible monster in the sense of it being a big scary thing.

More like it being something that will never exist.

A lot of projects have started up in the past to try and blend BSD and Linux systems.

Mostly they just die out from lack of interest. Mir OS was one, it was trying to make OpenBSD into a Linux. There was a pair of Debians that did it too, one for NetBSD and one for FreeBSD. There was a Gentoo NetBSD effort for a bit, but I don't think it ever got off the ground enough to make a single system running it.

The problem is that the two systems work similarly enough that no one sees a genuine advantage to trying them. The BSD users tend to be mostly happy with what they have and the Linux users tend to be mostly happy with what they have. The mix leaves both sides with shit they don't like.

Oh I know Ubuntu has been on a very anti-POSIX kick lately, and many are getting less happy with Ubuntu because of it. But I will wager most of them would be more happy just going with Mint or Debian.

I dunno, Gentoo did pretty well in general using the BSD concept of portage in a linux, and Gentoo FreeBSD is still active. Considering the amount of communication between the Ubuntu and Gentoo communities (mostly the Ubuntu people trying to get unusual things to work) however I agree that yeah, its not really very mainstream, so it will probably flounder around for a long time unless it gets some serious interest.
or you could just not use ubuntu

Good to see the effort simply because it encourages diversity in the *nix community. I am growing weary of all the calls for some kind of Grand Unified Linux. The power of Linux is in its diversity, though I will admit it's that same diversity that causes app developers fits.

However, I don't understand why they would try to replace the Linux kernel with FreeBSD. If there's anything truly awesome about Linux (the ecosystem) at this point it's the kernel and the manner in which it's developed. Tossing that great kernel simply to gain access to a single filesystem (ZFS) is retarded. ZFS is not is the second coming like so many people think it is. As someone who's run heavy-iron (very large scale enterprise/carrier grade Unix systems) I am more inclined to use hardware raid if I'm serious about not losing data. Any solution that lacks battery backed cache is a non-starter. Furthermore, the power of BSD is in the OS configuration, etc. which is refreshingly straightforward. If you want to run a BSD kernel or absolutely need ZFS for some reason, then run some flavor of BSD (Free, Open, etc.)
True, its not an absolute necessity here, but ZFS does have some really nice features, particularly the built in de-duplication and fast compression
